t: Timothy, and the letter's "we"
p: Timothy is named as co-sender, yet Paul often writes "I."
b: Timothy came from Lystra and joined Paul on his second journey (Acts 16:1–3). He helped found the church in Corinth (1:19; Acts 18:5) and Paul had sent him there once already (1 Corinthians 4:17; 16:10). The letter moves between "we" and "I" (compare 1:15 with 1:19, and 10:1). Some scholars take the "we" as Paul and his co-workers; others take most of it as an "epistolary plural" for Paul alone, a common habit in Greek letters (Thrall, Harris). Where the reader must decide, this Plain keeps the Greek person.
r: Acts 16:1–3; Acts 18:5; 1 Corinthians 4:17; 1 Corinthians 16:10; 1 Thessalonians 1:1; Philippians 1:1; Philemon 1:1

a: the church of God in Corinth
t: Corinth and "all Achaia"
p: The letter is for the church in Corinth and also for the believers around it.
b: Corinth was a Roman colony and the capital of the province of Achaia (southern Greece), where Gallio served as governor (Acts 18:12). The letter reaches past the city to "all the saints throughout Achaia." One such group was the church at Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern harbor (Romans 16:1). Athens, to the north, had a few believers too (Acts 17:34). Paul's first letter to Corinth also reached beyond the city, adding all who call on the name of the Lord in every place (1 Corinthians 1:2), though without naming Achaia. The wider address suggests that Paul expected the letter to be read, and perhaps copied, beyond the city.

t: "Apostle": a sent one with the sender's authority
p: Paul's right to be called an apostle is under attack in this letter.
b: Apostolos means someone sent out with the sender's authority. Paul opens with it because Corinthian critics have questioned him (3:1; 10:10; 11:5; 12:11–12). He rests his claim not on letters of recommendation (3:1) but on God's will and on the church itself, which he calls the "seal" of his apostleship (1 Corinthians 9:1–2). The opponents are a main puzzle of the letter: see the introduction and the later chapters. This Plain keeps "apostle" for the office, and uses "one who is sent" only where Paul means a church's messenger (8:23).

a: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ
t: A Jewish blessing at the head of a letter
p: Paul opens with the form of a Jewish prayer, not the usual Greek thanks.
b: Most of Paul's letters begin with thanks to God (1 Corinthians 1:4). Here, as in Ephesians 1:3 and 1 Peter 1:3, he begins instead with a "blessing," the Greek form of the Hebrew barukh, "Blessed be." Jewish prayers of this kind praise God for what he has done (Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:18; Luke 1:68). Paul keeps the Jewish shape but gives it a Christian center: God is now named by his relation to Jesus. The change from the usual thanks may mark how much relief and strain lie behind the letter (1:8–11; 7:5–7).
r: Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:18; Luke 1:68; Ephesians 1:3; 1 Peter 1:3; 1 Corinthians 1:4

t: "Comfort": one root, many English words
p: One Greek root runs through the letter. English has to choose among "comfort," "encourage" and "urge."
b: The noun paraklesis and the verb parakaleo appear well over twenty times in this letter, more than in any other letter of Paul. The root means calling someone alongside to help. It can mean comfort (1:4–7), encouragement, or an appeal (2:8; 5:20). The Plain gives "comfort" where the sense is comfort, and "urge" or "beg" where Paul appeals, but the reader should hear one word. The root is also behind the Advocate (parakletos) of John 14:16, and Isaiah 40:1 ("Comfort, comfort my people") lies behind Paul's idea that God's comfort comes at the turn of the age.

t: Whose sufferings are "the sufferings of Christ"?
p: Paul may mean Christ's own sufferings, or the sufferings believers share with him.
b: Three readings are held. (1) The sufferings Christ himself endured, which Paul shares by union with him (Philippians 3:10; Colossians 1:24). (2) The sufferings that come to anyone who follows Christ, so that believers' troubles are "Christ's" because they belong to him (Barrett, Thrall). (3) The "birth pains" of the end, a Jewish idea of a time of trouble before the new age, in which Christ's people are caught up (Mark 13:8; Allison). All three agree that suffering is the way comfort comes, and that comfort overflows to others (1:4, 6). The same pattern returns in 4:10–12.

t: "Brothers": men and women together
p: The Greek says "brothers," but Paul means the whole church, women included.
b: Adelphoi is the plural of "brother." Greek used the male plural for a mixed group, and Paul uses it for the whole congregation. The Plain keeps "brothers" as Acts and Romans do, so that the reader sees the Greek word, and it adds "brothers and sisters" in the Today's-words line. Paul names women among his co-workers and church members (Romans 16:1, 3, 7; Philippians 4:2–3), which makes the wider sense certain. Paul uses the word in this letter at 1:8, 8:1, 13:11 and elsewhere, often at a turning point when he wants his readers to listen.
r: Romans 1:13; Romans 16:1; Romans 16:3; Philippians 4:2–3; 2 Corinthians 8:1; 2 Corinthians 13:11

a: the trouble that came to us in Asia
t: What happened in Asia?
p: Paul almost died in the province of Asia. He does not say how, and scholars disagree.
b: "Asia" was the Roman province in western Turkey, with Ephesus as its capital. Paul had written 1 Corinthians from Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:8). Suggestions for the "trouble": a serious illness (Paul says only "death," 1:9); a plot or mob (the riot in Acts 19:23–41, though Paul was not hurt); a time in prison at Ephesus (Duncan, who points to 1 Corinthians 15:32 and Romans 16:4, where Prisca and Aquila "risked their necks"); or the whole run of hardships Paul lists later (11:23–27). Acts says nothing of a prison. The honest answer is that we do not know, and Paul wants the Corinthians to take the story as fact, not as a figure of speech.

t: A rare word for an official answer
p: Paul uses a legal word nobody else in the New Testament uses.
b: Apokrima appears only here in the New Testament. In Greek papyri it can mean an official reply or ruling, such as an emperor's answer to a petition. Paul says he received that sort of ruling "inside ourselves": he knew he was going to die. The KJV's "sentence of death" is close; the Plain says "verdict." Paul explains the reason in the next clause: the verdict was meant to break his trust in himself. The same pattern, power made perfect in weakness, is the theme of the letter (4:7; 12:9).

t: God who raises the dead
p: Paul's trust is in the God who brings the dead back to life.
b: The phrase is almost a title for God in Paul: Abraham trusted the God "who makes the dead alive" (Romans 4:17). Jewish worship has a similar line, in the second blessing of the Eighteen Benedictions (the Amidah, "who revives the dead"). The prayer's wording cannot be dated with certainty to Paul's day, so this is a comparison, not a source. For Paul the title is no longer only a hope about the last day. He met it when he was close to death, and the same God raised Jesus (4:14).

t: "Conscience": the inner witness
p: Paul calls his own conscience as a witness in his defense.
b: Syneidesis is literally "knowing with oneself," the inner voice that tells a person whether an act was right. Paul uses it often in 1 and 2 Corinthians (4:2; 5:11; 1 Corinthians 8:7–12; 1 Corinthians 10:25–29). Here it testifies for him against the charge that he plays fast and loose with his word (1:17). Elsewhere he is careful: a clear conscience does not settle the case, because God is the judge (1 Corinthians 4:4). This Plain renders the word "conscience" everywhere, as in Romans.
r: 2 Corinthians 4:2; 2 Corinthians 5:11; 1 Corinthians 4:4; 1 Corinthians 8:7; Romans 2:15; Romans 9:1

t: A "second grace": two visits, or a second blessing?
p: Paul had planned to visit twice, so that Corinth would be blessed twice.
b: Deutera charis, "a second grace," most likely means a second benefit: Paul had planned to come on the way to Macedonia and again on the way back (1:16), so that they would receive his visit twice. Westcott and Hort printed chara, "joy," here instead; most editions keep "grace." The matter at issue is Paul's travel plan, which the Corinthians had read as a sign that he cannot be trusted (1:17).

a: I meant to pass by way of you into Macedonia
t: Paul's changed travel plans
p: Paul changed his plans twice, and Corinth called him unreliable for it.
b: The sequence, pieced together from 1:15–16, 2:1 and 1 Corinthians 16:5–7, runs like this (a common reconstruction, not certain). Paul first planned to go from Ephesus to Corinth, on to Macedonia, back to Corinth, and then to Jerusalem (1:15–16). In 1 Corinthians 16:5–7 he announced a simpler route: Macedonia first, then Corinth. In between he made a short, painful visit (2:1; 13:2) and then chose not to return at once, to spare them (1:23). The Corinthians heard all this as "Yes" and "No" at the same time. The introduction to this letter gives the whole timeline.
r: 1 Corinthians 16:5–7; 2 Corinthians 2:1; 2 Corinthians 2:12–13; 2 Corinthians 7:5–7; 2 Corinthians 13:1–2; Acts 19:21; Acts 20:1–3

t: "Yes, yes" and "No, no"
p: A saying close to words of Jesus and of James about plain speech.
b: Paul asks whether he says "Yes, yes" and "No, no" at the same time, meaning that he promises one thing and does another. This site's Plain of Matthew 5:37 reads: "When you speak, say 'Yes, yes' or 'No, no.'" (Matthew 5:37), the same doubled form, and James 5:12 repeats it. Whether Paul knew that saying is not certain. Either way, the point is that a person of honest speech is not two-faced, and Paul uses it to move from his own plans to God's faithfulness (1:18). The doubling "Yes, yes" may mean an emphatic promise, or a quick change of mind.

a: For however many promises God has made
t: God's promises and the "Yes" in Christ
p: The promises meant here are the ones God made to Israel, now confirmed in Christ.
b: "Promises" (epaggeliai) in Paul regularly means God's promises to Israel in the Scriptures, above all to Abraham (Galatians 3:16; Romans 9:4; 15:8). Christians have often read the verse as saying that the promises were fulfilled in Christ and therefore passed to the church. Jewish and "Paul within Judaism" readers stress that Paul says Christ confirms the promises to the fathers (Romans 15:8), so that Gentiles share them without Israel losing them. Paul does not say here what happens to promises not yet kept (Romans 11:29). "Yes" and "Amen" are the same affirmation, in Greek and in Hebrew.

a: He is the one who anointed us
t: "Anointed": a hint of the name Christ
p: The Greek says "Christ" and "anointed" with the same root, and Paul hints at it.
b: Christ (Christos) means "anointed one," and the verb here (chrio) is from the same root. Paul has just said that God makes us firm "in Christ" (eis Christon) and "anointed" (chrisas) us. In Israel kings, priests and sometimes prophets were anointed with oil. Paul says that all believers share in the Anointed One's anointing, a thought found also in 1 John 2:20, 27. The Plain keeps "Christ" as a name in the letters, but a reader who knows the root hears the echo.
r: Exodus 29:7; 1 Samuel 16:13; Luke 4:18; 1 John 2:20; 1 John 2:27; Acts 10:38

t: The seal: baptism, ownership, or assurance?
p: A seal marked ownership. Churches differ on what Paul means by God's "seal" on believers.
b: In the ancient world a seal on a jar, a letter or a slave marked who owned it and protected it. Paul says God put his seal on believers (compare Ephesians 1:13; 4:30). Early Christian writers often took the seal to mean baptism, and the Catholic Church reads it so for baptism and confirmation (CCC 1274, 1295–1296). The Orthodox use "the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit" in chrismation after baptism. Reformed writers read it as God's pledge of assurance (Westminster Confession 18.2). Many Baptist and evangelical readers see the seal as the Spirit's gift at conversion itself. See also 5:5.

t: A down payment on what is still to come
p: The Greek word is a loan word for a down payment that guarantees the rest.
b: Arrabon is a business word borrowed from a Semitic language (compare Hebrew 'erabon). The Greek Old Testament uses it for the pledge Judah left with Tamar (Genesis 38:17–20). It was a first installment that bound the buyer to pay the whole price. Modern Greek still uses it for an engagement. Paul says the Spirit already given is that down payment of the inheritance still to come (5:5; Ephesians 1:14). English versions choose "pledge," "guarantee," "deposit" or "down payment." "Down payment" is the Plain's one rendering of this word here and in Ephesians 1:14, and it keeps both parts: it is real, and it is not yet all.

a: I call God as my witness
t: Does Paul swear an oath?
p: Paul calls God as witness, which looks like an oath, though Jesus warned against oaths.
b: Paul's words follow the pattern of a solemn oath (compare Romans 1:9; Galatians 1:20). In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says, "do not take oaths at all" (Matthew 5:34), and James repeats it (James 5:12). The churches have answered differently. The Anabaptist tradition has refused oaths on the strength of Jesus's words (Schleitheim Confession, article 7); Quakers also refuse them. Most others hold that Jesus forbids careless or false swearing, not the truthful oath in court (Westminster Confession 22). Many point to Paul as one case where the apostle speaks as under oath.

a: I would not come to you again in grief
t: The painful visit
p: Paul made a short visit that went badly, between the two letters we have.
b: "Again" suggests that an earlier visit had brought grief. Acts does not tell of it. The clues are here and in 12:14, 13:1–2 ("this is the third time I am coming," and "I warned you when I was present the second time"). Most scholars place a brief, painful visit from Ephesus to Corinth after 1 Corinthians, in which someone publicly insulted or wronged Paul (2:5; 7:12) and the church failed to defend him. A minority (Hughes) read "again" differently: there was no painful visit, and Paul spared them a second visit that would have brought grief. The timeline in this chapter's study page sets out the options.

t: The letter written "through many tears"
p: Paul wrote a hard letter after the painful visit. It may be lost, or it may be in this book.
b: This "tearful letter" (also called the severe letter) is not 1 Corinthians, say most modern scholars, because 1 Corinthians does not fit the description of a letter written in anguish to settle a personal injury (2:3–4; 7:8–12). Titus most likely carried it (7:6–7, 13–15), though Paul does not say so in so many words. Three views: (1) it is lost (Barrett, Furnish, Thrall, Harris); (2) it is 1 Corinthians (an older view, held by Hughes and some others); (3) it survives as chapters 10–13, which are harsh and sound like the letter (proposed by Hausrath in 1870, developed by Kennedy and Bornkamm). Chapter 10 begins the part of this debate that bears on the shape of 2 Corinthians.

t: Who is the offender?
p: Someone wronged Paul or his authority. Scholars disagree on who he was.
b: Paul does not name him. The older view, common before the 1800s, held that he was the man of 1 Corinthians 5:1–5 who lived with his father's wife, now repentant. Most modern scholars reject this. Paul speaks of a wrongdoer and a person wronged (7:12), and the injury seems to have been to Paul himself or to a representative of his, perhaps at the painful visit (Barrett, Furnish, Thrall). A third view says the offender led the revolt against Paul at Corinth. The church punished him "by the majority" (2:6), and Paul asks them to stop. The point for readers is the pattern: discipline, repentance, forgiveness.

t: "In the person of Christ" or "before Christ"?
p: The Latin translation led the Catholic Church to read this as forgiveness given in Christ's place.
b: The Greek is en prosopo Christou, literally "in the face of Christ," which most take as "in the presence of Christ," under his eyes (compare 4:6). The Latin Vulgate translated it in persona Christi, "in the person of Christ," and the KJV followed it ("in the person of Christ"). Catholic teaching has used that wording for the priest who forgives sins as Christ's representative (Council of Trent, session 14; CCC 1441–1442, 1461). The Greek word can mean face, person or presence, and Eastern Christians who read the Greek and most Protestant commentators take it as "in the presence of." See the card on this page.

a: so that Satan will not take advantage of us
t: "Take advantage of": Satan as a swindler
p: The Greek word is about greed and cheating. Satan wins when a church will not forgive.
b: Pleonekteo means to get more than one's share, to cheat or exploit. In 12:17–18 Paul uses it of money. Here the one who would cheat the church is Satan, and he does it two ways: by driving an offender into despair (2:7) or by splitting the church over forgiveness. Paul says "we are not ignorant of what he has in mind." The Greek word for "what he has in mind" (noemata, thoughts or schemes) is used again of the minds that were hardened (3:14) or blinded (4:4) and of the "thoughts" Paul takes captive (10:5). Satan is named again in 11:14 and 12:7.

t: Troas, a harbor on the way
p: Troas was a Roman port city on the northwest coast of Turkey.
b: Troas was a seaport on the Aegean, the usual crossing point between Asia and Macedonia. Paul passed through it on his second journey, when the vision of the Macedonian man called him over to Greece (Acts 16:8–11), and again later, when he restored Eutychus (Acts 20:5–12). Here he came to preach and found "a door" open (compare 1 Corinthians 16:9; Colossians 4:3), but he could not stay, because Titus, who most likely had taken the severe letter to Corinth, had not come with news. Paul left for Macedonia to meet him (7:5–6).

t: Titus, the go-between
p: Titus carried Paul's hard letter to Corinth and brought back news.
b: Titus, a Greek convert whom Paul would not have circumcised (Galatians 2:1–3), appears only in Paul's letters (not in Acts). He most likely carried the severe letter to Corinth and was to return and meet Paul (7:6–7). He is the man who then goes ahead to organize the collection (8:6, 16–17; 12:18). Paul's restless anxiety here, enough to leave an open door, shows how much he feared that his break with Corinth was permanent. It is one of the most personal moments in the letter. The story picks up again at 7:5.
r: Galatians 2:1–3; 2 Corinthians 7:5–7; 2 Corinthians 8:6; 2 Corinthians 8:16–17; 2 Corinthians 12:18; Titus 1:4

a: leads us in his victory parade
t: The Roman triumph: is Paul a general or a captive?
p: Paul pictures a Roman victory parade. Scholars disagree on where he stands in it.
b: Thriambeuo comes from thriambos, the Greek form of the Roman triumphus, in which a victorious general led his army, his captives and the spoils through the city, with incense burned in the temples and along the way (Plutarch, Aemilius Paullus 32). Josephus describes the one that Vespasian and Titus held in Rome in AD 71 for the conquest of Jerusalem (Jewish War 7.121–157), where the enemy leader Simon was executed at the end. Views: (1) Paul is a captive, led to death in the train of Christ's victory (Hafemann, Marshall; this fits 4:7–12); (2) Paul is a soldier or sharer in the victory, an honor and not a humiliation; (3) the verb only means "cause to triumph," with Christ as the one who triumphs and Paul as his instrument. Commentators weigh these differently. The Plain keeps "victory parade," which allows each reading.

t: A sweet perfume for God, a smell of death for others
p: The same fragrance means life to some and death to others.
b: Paul moves from the incense of the parade to the sacrifice. "Sweet perfume" (euodia) is the Greek Old Testament's "soothing aroma" that rises from an offering (Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9; Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 4:18). The same message of the cross is received as life by some and as death by others, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 1:18, 23. The Jewish saying that Torah is for some a "drug of life" and for others a "drug of death" (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 72b) is a comparison, not a source; it shows that the double effect of God's word was a known idea. The question "who is up to this task?" (2:16) leads into chapter 3.
r: Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9; Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 4:18; 1 Corinthians 1:18; 1 Corinthians 1:23

t: "Peddle": the tradesman who waters the wine
p: The Greek word is a tavern-keeper or small trader who cheats, a common insult for traveling teachers.
b: Kapeleuo comes from kapelos, a huckster or small retailer, and was used of those who sold goods dishonestly (for instance by watering wine). Greek writers used it as an insult for traveling teachers who charged fees. Paul takes his meaning from his Corinthian critics, who thought that he should have accepted payment and that he looked weak when he did not (11:7–11; 12:13; 1 Corinthians 9:12–18). Paul's answer is that his work is "sincere," free of mixed motives, from God and before God. The Plain does not add "for profit," which is in the word's sense, not in the Greek.

t: Letters of recommendation
p: In the ancient world a traveling teacher carried letters that vouched for him.
b: Letters of recommendation were ordinary in the Greek world and in the church. Apollos left Ephesus for Achaia with a letter from the believers there (Acts 18:27), Phoebe was commended in writing (Romans 16:1–2), and Paul himself once carried letters from the high priest (Acts 9:2). Some other teachers had come to Corinth with such letters (3:1; compare 10:12, 18; 11:4), and the Corinthians had begun to ask for Paul's. He answers with a surprising image: the church itself is his letter. Nothing in his reply condemns the practice; Paul writes his own recommendations (1 Corinthians 16:3; Romans 16:1–2).
r: Acts 9:2; Acts 18:27; Romans 16:1–2; 1 Corinthians 16:3; 2 Corinthians 10:12; 2 Corinthians 10:18

a: tablets that are hearts of flesh
t: Stone tablets and hearts of flesh
p: Paul joins three Old Testament pictures: the stone tablets, the written heart, and the new heart.
b: The "tablets of stone" are the Ten Words that God wrote (Exodus 31:18; 34:1). "Written on hearts" echoes Jeremiah's new covenant: "I will put my law inside them, and on their hearts I will write it" (Jeremiah 31:33). "Hearts of flesh" echoes Ezekiel: "I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 36:26). Ezekiel goes on to promise God's own Spirit inside them (Ezekiel 36:27). Paul has fused two promises, both made to Israel, and applies them to a mostly Gentile church, whose changed lives show what God has done. The Greek has "fleshly," and Paul means the word as good news here, not as the bad sense in 1:12.
r: Exodus 31:18; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26–27; Proverbs 3:3; Proverbs 7:3; Deuteronomy 6:6

t: "New covenant": Jeremiah's promise to Israel
p: The new covenant comes from Jeremiah 31 and was first promised to Israel and Judah.
b: Jeremiah wrote: "Look, days are coming, the LORD declares, when I will cut a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah" (Jeremiah 31:31). The promise is that God's law will be written on the heart and sins forgiven (31:33–34). Paul uses the exact phrase only here and at 1 Corinthians 11:25, the Lord's Supper; Hebrews 8:8–13 quotes Jeremiah at length. Views: (1) the church is the new covenant community, replacing the Mosaic covenant (the traditional Christian reading, with Hebrews 8:13); (2) the new covenant renews and completes God's covenant with Israel, in which Gentiles share (Wright, Dunn); (3) Paul speaks to Gentiles about their own place and says nothing about the covenant of Israel (some "Paul within Judaism" readers, a school associated with Gager and Nanos). Jewish readers have usually taken Jeremiah's "new" to mean the same Torah written on the heart, not a replacement. See the cards at 3:6 and 3:14.
r: Jeremiah 31:31–34; Ezekiel 36:26–27; Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25; Hebrews 8:6–13; Hebrews 10:15–18; Romans 11:27

a: For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
t: "The letter kills": five readings
p: Paul does not say the Law is evil. What he means by "letter" has been argued since the early church.
b: Gramma, "letter," means something written. Readings: (1) the literal sense of Scripture, against a spiritual or allegorical one (Origen). (2) The Law without the grace to keep it, a view Augustine developed in On the Spirit and the Letter (AD 412): the Law commands, the Spirit enables. (3) The Law as condemning, against the gospel (Luther, Lutheran confessions). (4) The Mosaic covenant as a whole, whose stone tablets could pronounce the sentence on a stubborn people but not change their hearts (Hafemann, Wright). (5) A contrast between Paul's own ministry and that of rivals, with no statement about Judaism at all (suggested by some "Paul within Judaism" readers). Paul's grammar and the Exodus background (3:7–11) favor the middle readings. See the card.
r: Romans 2:29; Romans 7:6; Romans 8:2; Deuteronomy 30:6; Ezekiel 11:19–20; Exodus 32:28

t: Why is the Sinai ministry called "death"?
p: Paul remembers the golden calf, when the tablets were broken and many died.
b: Paul's phrase "ministry of death" is not a general attack on the Law, which he calls "holy" elsewhere (Romans 7:12). The most likely background is Exodus 32–34. The tablets were given, and then the people made the golden calf. Moses broke the tablets, and about three thousand died (Exodus 32:28). God said that he could not go with them lest he destroy them (Exodus 33:3). Paul's argument is from the lesser to the greater: if even this ministry, which ended in judgment on a stiff-necked people, came with glory, the ministry of the Spirit has more. Hafemann builds his book on this reading.
r: Exodus 32:19; Exodus 32:28; Exodus 33:3; Exodus 34:1; Romans 7:12; Romans 7:10

t: Moses, the shining face, and the horns
p: Paul's story follows Exodus 34, but the Hebrew word for "shone" gave medieval art Moses with horns.
b: Exodus 34:29 says: "the skin of his face was shining." The Hebrew verb qaran is rare and comes from qeren, "horn." Aquila, an early Jewish translator into Greek, understood the verb as "became horned," and Jerome's Latin Vulgate wrote cornuta esset facies sua, "his face was horned." That is why Michelangelo's Moses has horns. Most scholars take the Hebrew to mean rays of light, like horns of light. Paul works from the Greek Old Testament, which says "the appearance of the skin of his face was glorified," and reads the story in the light of 3:13.

a: a glory that was being set aside
t: "Set aside": faded, ended, or made powerless?
p: One Greek verb in 3:7, 11, 13 and 14 can be heard as fade, end, or lose power. The Plain uses a word that leaves the choice open.
b: Katargeo is passive in all four places (3:7, 11, 13, 14): the glory, "what was being set aside," and the thing that "is being set aside" in Christ are acted on. In Paul the verb means to make idle or ineffective, or to bring to an end (Romans 3:31; 6:6; 1 Corinthians 15:24, 26). One question runs through the four places: what does Paul say is happening to the glory? Answers: (1) it fades, a slow loss, so that Moses hid the fading (a common reading, though Exodus 34 never says the glory faded and the reading looks unflattering to Moses); (2) it comes to an end by design, because it was always meant to give way to something greater; (3) it is made powerless, its power to condemn cancelled as the ministry of condemnation gives way to the ministry of the Spirit. English cannot give all three, so the Plain says "set aside" in all four places, which is neutral between fading and abolishing. In 3:14, "because in Christ it is being set aside," the "it" is not named: it can be the veil, the old covenant, or the old order (see the variant at 3:14). Why Moses wore the veil is a separate question, taken up at 3:13. The "passed away" of 5:17 translates a different verb, parerchomai.
r: Exodus 34:33–35; Romans 3:31; Romans 6:6; Romans 7:2; 1 Corinthians 13:8–10; 1 Corinthians 15:24–26

a: put a veil over his face
t: Why did Moses wear the veil?
p: Exodus says he veiled his face when he was not speaking with God. Paul gives a different reason.
b: In Exodus 34:33 Moses put the veil on after speaking with the people: "When Moses finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face" (Exodus 34:33). Exodus gives no reason for it except that the people were afraid (34:30). Paul says it was "so that the Israelites would not look steadily at the end of what was being set aside." Views: (1) to hide the fading from the people (the common reading); (2) to keep the people from seeing the glory, as an act of mercy, since the sight would destroy a stubborn people (Hafemann); (3) telos means "goal," and the veil kept Israel from seeing that Christ is the goal of the Law (compare Romans 10:4). Paul also turns the veil into a picture for Israel's minds (3:14).

t: "Hardened": the callus word
p: Paul uses a word for a callus that has lost feeling. He uses it again of Israel in Romans.
b: Poroo comes from poros, a hard stone or callus, and means to make insensitive or stubborn. Mark uses it of the disciples (Mark 6:52) and of Pharisees (Mark 3:5), John of the unbelief in Isaiah 6 (John 12:40), and Paul of "the rest" of Israel in Romans 11:7, 25. There the hardening is partial and temporary, "until the full number of the Gentiles comes in." Here too the verse ends with hope (3:16). Paul's grief for his own people (Romans 9:1–3) should be read along with the harsh word. Later Christian use of it against Jews as a whole goes far beyond what Paul says.
r: Mark 3:5; Mark 6:52; John 12:40; Romans 11:7; Romans 11:25; Romans 9:1–3

t: "Old covenant": the only place Paul says it
p: This is the only New Testament use of the phrase, and it does not say "abolished."
b: Palaia diatheke, "old covenant," appears only here in the New Testament. The name "Old Testament" for a collection of books came later. For Paul it is what is "read" when "Moses is read" (3:15), the writings of Moses in synagogue worship. "Old" (palaios) can mean ancient and honored, not worn out; Hebrews calls the first covenant "old" and "obsolete" (Hebrews 8:13), which says more. Whether Paul means the Mosaic covenant has ended (for all, or for those in Christ), or that Israel still reads it and misses what it points to, is argued. See the card.
r: Hebrews 8:13; Hebrews 9:15; Romans 9:4; Romans 11:28–29; Galatians 4:24; 2 Corinthians 3:15

t: Moses went in, and the veil came off
p: Paul takes Exodus 34:34 and makes it a picture of anyone who turns to the Lord.
b: Paul is quoting and reworking Exodus 34:34, which in this site's Plain says: "But whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he took the veil off until he came out." The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb for "take away" that Paul uses here. The "Lord" in Exodus is YHWH; for Paul, "the Lord" is usually Christ, but 3:17 may indicate that he is reading "the Lord" in Exodus as the Spirit. Anyone who turns to the Lord, as Moses did, enters the place where the veil is gone. The text's "whenever" is for repeated turning, not a single event.

t: "The Lord is the Spirit": what does it identify?
p: Paul does not simply say that Christ and the Spirit are the same person.
b: Views: (1) Exegetical: "the Lord" is the Lord of Exodus 34:34, and Paul says that this "Lord" means the Spirit, as if to say "that word stands for the Spirit" (Thrall, Harris and many commentators). (2) Functional: Paul means that the risen Lord Jesus and the Spirit are not experienced apart; where one is, the other is (Dunn). (3) Trinitarian readings: the verse does not erase the persons, as is shown by "the Spirit of the Lord" in the same verse and by "from the Lord, who is the Spirit" in 3:18, which many read as "from the Lord of the Spirit." The Plain's "from the Lord, who is the Spirit" is one of three ways to read the Greek (the Lord who is the Spirit; the Lord of the Spirit; the Spirit of the Lord) and leans toward the first view above. The Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant churches all hold the Trinity and read the verse accordingly.

t: A mirror: looking, or reflecting?
p: The Greek verb can mean looking in a mirror or acting as a mirror, and the choice changes the image.
b: Katoptrizomai is used in the middle voice. It can mean "look at ourselves in a mirror" or "look at as in a mirror," or "reflect, like a mirror." The Plain follows the second: we see the Lord's glory indirectly, as in a polished bronze mirror, a familiar object in the Greek world. Corinth was known for its bronze work, and some wonder whether that lies behind the picture; that link is a possibility, not something Paul says. Compare 1 Corinthians 13:12, which also speaks of seeing in a mirror, dimly. Those who favor "reflect" point to the picture of Moses's face as a mirror of God's glory and of the church as a face that gives it back to others.

t: "From glory to glory": transformation
p: Eastern Christianity builds its idea of union with God partly on this verse.
b: The change "into the same image" is the image of the Lord (4:4) and of God (Genesis 1:26–27; Colossians 3:10; Romans 8:29). Paul says it happens as we look, and "from glory to glory" is a process. Orthodox writers, such as Gregory of Nyssa, read it as an endless growth toward God, and call the goal theosis, sharing God's life. Catholic teaching speaks of divinization by grace (CCC 460, 1999). Reformed and Lutheran readers stress the restoring of the image and growth in holiness. Wesley's followers read it as growth toward perfect love. See the card.

t: "Falsify": mixing in what does not belong
p: A rare verb. It means to tamper, as a merchant waters down wine or mixes in cheap metal.
b: Doloo appears only here in the New Testament. It means to adulterate or falsify, to make a pure thing impure by mixing something into it. Paul's reply to the charge of trickery (compare 12:16, where the charge is "crafty") is that his open statement of the truth is its own recommendation to every person's conscience. The Corinthians' real question may be why his "plain truth" has such weak results. Paul answers in 4:3–4: the fault lies with a veil, not with the message.

t: Who is "the god of this age"?
p: Paul calls Satan a "god" only here. Some early Christians read the verse differently.
b: Nearly all modern commentators read this as Satan, who rules the present age that is passing away (compare John 12:31; 14:30; 1 Corinthians 2:6–8; Galatians 1:4; Ephesians 2:2). The calling of a rebellious power "god" fits a Jewish idea of two ages, and Qumran's picture of the Angel of Darkness who leads the righteous astray (1QS 3:20–24) is a close parallel in thought. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.7.1) and Tertullian (Against Marcion 5.11) read it differently because heretics (Marcion, Gnostics) used the verse to say that the Creator was an evil god: they put a pause after "God" and read "God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age." Paul says elsewhere that there is one God (1 Corinthians 8:4–6). See the card.
r: John 12:31; John 14:30; 1 Corinthians 2:6–8; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6; Galatians 1:4; Ephesians 2:2; Ephesians 6:12

a: who is the image of God
t: Christ, the image of God
p: Christ is called God's image, the role the Bible gave to Adam.
b: Genesis says that humans were made in God's image (Genesis 1:26–27). Paul calls Christ "the image of God" (eikon), and the believers' goal is to be changed into that image (3:18; Romans 8:29). Colossians 1:15 says the same, perhaps from the Jewish idea of Wisdom as the image of God's goodness (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26). The thought is of Christ as the true Adam who shows what a human being was meant to be. Seyoon Kim suggests that the language of "light" and "glory" in 4:4–6 comes from Paul's Damascus-road meeting with the glorified Christ (Acts 9:3; 22:6).
r: Genesis 1:26–27; Colossians 1:15; Romans 8:29; Hebrews 1:3; Wisdom of Solomon 7:26; Acts 9:3

t: "Shine on them": see clearly, or shine?
p: The rare Greek verb can mean to see clearly or to shine out. Paul's sentence works either way.
b: Augazo is rare, and it is used in the New Testament only here. It can mean "to see clearly, to catch sight of," which gives "so that they cannot see the light of the good news." It can also mean "to shine forth," which gives "so that the light of the good news cannot shine." The Plain follows the second. Both fit a verse about blindness and light, and 4:6 answers it with God who "shone in our hearts."

t: "Slave": Paul's word for himself and for Christ's servants
p: Paul calls himself the Corinthians' slave for Jesus's sake, which is a bold thing to say to a status-minded church.
b: Doulos means a slave, someone owned. Paul uses it of his relation to Christ (Romans 1:1) and here of his relation to the church. The word is bolder than English "servant," and in Corinth, where honor and rank mattered, it was shocking: the apostle puts himself below the people he serves. He is not their slave in the sense that they own him, but "for Jesus' sake": the one who rules him is Christ. The Plain keeps "slave" for doulos and uses "servant" only for diakonos (3:6; 6:4; 11:23).

a: Out of darkness light will shine
t: Light out of darkness
p: Paul's words are close to Genesis 1:3 but are not an exact quotation.
b: This site's Plain of Genesis 1:3 reads: "Then God said, 'Let there be light.' And light came to be." Paul's words ("Out of darkness light will shine") match neither the Hebrew nor the Greek text of Genesis. Some think he combines it with Isaiah 9:2 or Psalm 112:4, or that he paraphrases from memory. The thought is plain: the God who made light on the first day has made light in the heart, as at the new creation (5:17). Kim and others add that Paul is thinking of his own conversion, when the glory of Christ shone on him (Acts 9:3–5).

t: A treasure in clay pots
p: Plain jars of baked clay held valuables. Paul's body is the plain container.
b: Ostrakinos means made of baked clay. Such jars were cheap, easily broken and everywhere. They also stored valuables: Jeremiah was told to put a deed in a clay jar "so that they will last for many days" (Jeremiah 32:14), and the Dead Sea Scrolls were found in jars. The Bible often calls humans clay (Job 10:9; Isaiah 64:8; Romans 9:21). Another suggestion is Gideon's jars, broken so that light could shine out (Judges 7:19–20). Paul's point is plain: the message is precious, the carrier is fragile, and the fragility shows that the power is God's. Fitzgerald notes that Paul's lists of hardship in Corinth reverse the Stoic ideal of the unshaken wise man.
r: Jeremiah 32:14; Job 10:9; Isaiah 64:8; Judges 7:19–20; Romans 9:21; 2 Corinthians 12:9–10

t: A list of hardships in four pairs
p: Paul writes a poem of four pairs, each with a hardship and a reason it does not win.
b: Lists of hardships (peristaseis) were a known form: Stoic writers, such as Seneca in Paul's day and Epictetus a generation later, listed the troubles a wise man bore without being shaken (Fitzgerald). Paul uses the form but changes it, since he does not claim to be above hardship: he is hard pressed, at a loss, hunted and knocked down. Each is matched with a limit: not crushed, not in despair, not abandoned, not destroyed. Similar lists appear at 6:4–10, 11:23–29 and 12:10, and 1 Corinthians 4:9–13. The "but not" is not a boast but a testimony to God.

t: Carrying the dying of Jesus
p: Paul says he carries the "dying" of Jesus in his body. He means his own daily danger.
b: Nekrosis means a putting to death, and the process of dying. It is used in the New Testament only here and of the "deadness" of Sarah's womb (Romans 4:19). Paul does not mean that he suffers Christ's atoning death; he means that his own daily dangers match the pattern of Jesus's death, and that Jesus's life shows in the rescue. Compare Galatians 6:17, where he carries "the marks of Jesus" on his body. The Corinthians boast of strength; Paul says the cross shows in the apostle's weakness (13:4).

t: Psalm 116:10 in Greek and in Hebrew
p: Paul quotes the Greek form of Psalm 116:10. The Hebrew says something different.
b: The Greek Old Testament (Psalm 115:1) reads "I believed, therefore I spoke," and Paul quotes it. This site's Plain of the Hebrew says: "I kept trusting, even when I said, 'I am bowed down very low'" (Psalm 116:10). In both the psalmist speaks from affliction and stays faithful. Paul uses it for his own suffering: the one who trusts, speaks, even in danger. The psalm goes on to a song of thanks for rescue from death (Psalm 116:3–9), and Paul writes the next verse about resurrection (4:14).

t: The outer and the inner person
p: Paul's "inner person" is not Plato's immortal soul.
b: Plato had spoken of "the inner human being" (Republic 589a), and some readers find Greek dualism in Paul's words. Paul uses the pair in his own way: the "outer" person is the self as it ages and wastes away, and the "inner" is the self being renewed by the Spirit (Romans 7:22; Ephesians 3:16). He does not say that the body is evil or that the soul is naturally immortal; he looks to a new body (5:1; 1 Corinthians 15:42–49). The contrast is between two ages. The "outer" person belongs to the old age that is passing away, the "inner" to the new.
orig: ὁ ἔξω ἄνθρωπος / ὁ ἔσω (ho exo anthropos / ho eso)

a: a weight of glory beyond all measure
t: A "weight" of glory: a Hebrew wordplay?
p: The Hebrew word for glory also means "weight," and some think Paul is playing on it.
b: Paul's phrase is "a weight of glory" (baros doxes). The Hebrew kabod means both "glory" and "heaviness" (from kabed, to be heavy), and many commentators see Paul, who thought in Hebrew, playing on this. It is a suggestion, not a certainty, since Paul writes in Greek. The point is a scale: on one side "trouble" that is "slight" and "momentary"; on the other a glory heavy beyond measure and lasting forever. Paul has just written of trouble that nearly killed him (1:8) and will list worse (11:23–29), so "slight" is chosen on purpose, as a judgment of faith.

t: The tent for the body
p: Paul calls the body a tent, a picture also found in Wisdom of Solomon and in Peter.
b: The body as a "tent" (skenos) appears in Wisdom of Solomon 9:15 ("the earthly tent weighs down the mind"; that book is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians), in 2 Peter 1:13–14, and in Hezekiah's complaint, "My home is pulled up and carried off from me like a herder's tent" (Isaiah 38:12). The picture suits Paul, who made tents (Acts 18:3), and he may also be thinking of Israel's wilderness tent, the Tabernacle, and of the temple as a dwelling of God (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19). A tent is a place for passing through, and not a permanent home.
r: Wisdom of Solomon 9:15; 2 Peter 1:13–14; Isaiah 38:12; Acts 18:3; 1 Corinthians 6:19

a: a house made by no human hands
t: What is the building from God?
p: The "building" has been read as a resurrection body, a heavenly dwelling, or the church.
b: The adjective acheiropoietos, "not made by hands," is used of the new temple Jesus would raise (Mark 14:58) and of the new circumcision (Colossians 2:11); Hebrews says God's tabernacle is "not made with hands" (Hebrews 9:11, 24). Four readings of 5:1: (1) the resurrection body, given at the end (Wright); (2) a heavenly body received at death, before the final resurrection (Harris, in Raised Immortal, 1983); (3) a corporate house, the body of Christ or the church (Ellis); (4) heaven itself, a place and not a body. Whether Paul changed his mind between 1 Corinthians 15 and 2 Corinthians 5 after nearly dying (1:8–9) was suggested by Dodd and is much argued. See the card on 5:8.
r: Mark 14:58; Colossians 2:11; Hebrews 9:11; Hebrews 9:24; 1 Corinthians 15:42–54; Philippians 1:21–23

a: If we are indeed dressed, we will not be found naked.
t: Dressed or undressed, and what is "naked"?
p: Two readings, "having put on" or "having taken off," change the sentence. Then "naked" has its own puzzle.
b: See the variant on this verse for the manuscripts. "Naked" has been taken to mean: a soul without a body (the Greek picture in Plato, Gorgias 523–524, where souls are judged "naked"); standing exposed in shame at the judgment (Genesis 3:7–10); or those not clothed with Christ (Galatians 3:27). Paul's worry looks like the first or second. Nakedness was a Jewish shame, and Paul does not look forward to being an unclothed soul. He hopes to be "dressed over" with the new body, as in 1 Corinthians 15:53–54, where "this mortal must put on immortality."
r: Genesis 3:7; Genesis 3:21; 1 Corinthians 15:51–54; Galatians 3:27; Revelation 3:18; Revelation 16:15

t: "At home" and "away": the language of citizenship
p: Paul plays on the Greek words for living in one's own land and for being abroad.
b: Endemeo means to be at home, in one's own demos (district or people), and ekdemeo means to be away, abroad. Paul's picture: while we live in the body we are like travelers away from the home country where the Lord is. Philippians 3:20 says the same thing in another way: "our citizenship is in heaven." Paul is not saying the body is a prison, since he longs for a new one (5:2). The point is that the Lord's presence is not yet complete here: we "walk by faith" and not by sight (5:7).

a: away from the body and at home with the Lord
t: Between death and resurrection
p: Paul seems to expect to be with the Lord at death. Churches differ on what that state is.
b: Paul says here, and in Philippians 1:23 ("to depart and be with Christ, which is far better"), that death brings him to the Lord. Yet 1 Corinthians 15 puts the resurrection of the body at Christ's return, and 5:1–4 says he does not wish to be "unclothed." The questions: Is the dead person conscious? Does the person have a body? Is there a time gap? Views are set out in the card. In this chapter's study page the main scholarly options (immediate embodiment, an interim "unclothed" state, and a view in which time is not measured the same way after death) are explained.

t: "Ambition": love of honor
p: The Greek verb is about love of honor, the driving force of a Roman city like Corinth.
b: Philotimeomai comes from philotimia, "love of honor," a leading civic virtue: wealthy citizens competed to pay for buildings, games and gifts, and had their names carved on them (Danker). Paul uses it only here, in Romans 15:20 and in 1 Thessalonians 4:11. He takes the Corinthian love of honor and points it at a single judge: to please Christ "whether at home or away." Seeking honor from the church or from the rivals who boast of appearances (5:12) is then beside the point.

t: The bema: a platform in Corinth's forum
p: The "judgment seat" was a raised platform where a Roman official heard cases. Corinth had one.
b: Bema is the raised platform from which a magistrate gave verdicts. At Corinth, Gallio sat on one when the Jews brought Paul before him (Acts 18:12–17), and the remains of a large platform in the Corinthian forum can be seen today (its exact date is debated). Paul uses the same word for Christ's court in Romans 14:10. Everyone will appear there, "each one" for what was done "through the body." Paul does not say here whether the judgment concerns reward only or can also condemn. Churches differ (see the card).

t: "Out of our minds": ecstasy, or an insult?
p: Paul may be answering the charge that he is mad, or he may mean his speaking in tongues.
b: Existemi means to be out of one's senses. Jesus's family said the same of him (Mark 3:21), and Festus called Paul mad (Acts 26:24). Two readings: (1) the Corinthians mocked Paul as a fanatic and Paul turns the charge around: if he is mad, it is for God (Barrett); (2) he refers to his ecstatic experiences, such as speaking in tongues (1 Corinthians 14:18) and the vision of 12:1–4, which he keeps private. The second half "if we are thinking clearly, it is for you" speaks of the plain teaching he gives them.

a: one died for all, and so all died
t: "All died": substitution or inclusion?
p: If one died for all, did all die with him? Scholars answer in two ways.
b: The Greek says "one died for (hyper) all; therefore all died." Readings: (1) Substitution: Christ died in the place of all, so that all, in him, have undergone the penalty of death (the traditional reading in much of Western theology; some Reformed readers take the second "all" as "all who are his"). (2) Inclusion or participation: all who are in Christ died with him to the old age (Hooker's "interchange," Wright, Gorman); this leads straight into 5:15 and Romans 6:3–8. The second half of 5:15, "no longer live for themselves," fits the second reading. Who counts as "all" is the question of the extent of the atonement; see the card.
r: Romans 5:6–8; Romans 6:3–8; Galatians 2:19–20; Colossians 3:3; 1 Timothy 2:6; Hebrews 2:9

a: know no one by the flesh
t: "According to the flesh": a way of knowing
p: Paul does not say he never met the earthly Jesus. He says he no longer judges by outward standards.
b: Kata sarka, "by the flesh," can describe the one known or the way of knowing. Older readers took the verse as saying that Paul had seen Jesus in the flesh, or that he saw Jesus before Damascus as a false messiah. Most today (Bultmann, Martyn, Thrall) hold that it describes the way of knowing: by outward measures such as status, power and appearance, the measures the Corinthians used to rank apostles (5:12; 10:7). Since the cross and resurrection, Paul says, he judges by the new creation. The sentence does not decide how much Paul knew of Jesus's earthly life; compare 1 Corinthians 7:10 and 11:23.

t: "New creation": person, church, or world?
p: The Greek has no verb: "if anyone in Christ, new creation." The KJV's "he is a new creature" adds more than the Greek says.
b: Three readings. (1) The individual is made new (the KJV and traditional preaching). (2) The whole world is being made new, with the believer seeing it begin (Martyn and other "apocalyptic" readers; compare Galatians 6:15). (3) The community, the new humanity of Jew and Gentile (Hubbard). Wright reads the phrase within the covenant story of Israel's restoration, and so does not choose just one of these. The background is Isaiah's promise of "new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17) and God's word in Isaiah 43:19, "Look at me, about to do something new" (Isaiah 43:19). Jewish writings speak of a "new creation" at the end (Jubilees 4:26; 1 Enoch 72:1; both are Scripture for the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo church), and later rabbis said a convert is like "a newborn child" (Yevamot 22a); these are comparisons that show the language was in the air.
r: Isaiah 43:18–19; Isaiah 65:17; Isaiah 66:22; Galatians 6:15; Romans 8:19–23; Jubilees 4:26; 1 Enoch 72:1

t: "Reconcile": Paul's own word for peace with God
p: Paul's word comes from personal and political life. In Greek religion people tried to appease the gods, not the reverse.
b: Katallasso means to change from enmity to friendship; Greek writers used it for spouses, for friends and for states. In Greek religion, humans tried to win over a god. Paul says that God is the one who acts (Breytenbach). The word appears in 5:18–20, Romans 5:10–11 and Colossians 1:20–22. In 2 Maccabees, which is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, people pray that God will "be reconciled" to them (2 Maccabees 1:5; 7:33), so Paul's reversal (God reconciles us) stands out. Who is reconciled to whom: the world to God, or God to the world? Paul says here that God is not changed; he is the one reconciling.
r: Romans 5:10–11; Colossians 1:20–22; Ephesians 2:16; 2 Maccabees 1:5; 2 Maccabees 7:33; 2 Maccabees 8:29

a: God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself
t: "God was in Christ": two ways to read the Greek
p: The sentence can mean that God was present in Christ, or that God was reconciling in Christ.
b: The Greek theos en en Christo kosmon katallasson heauto is a periphrasis. It can be read as: (1) "God was in Christ, reconciling the world" (God present in the person of Christ; used in discussions of Christ's divinity and the incarnation); or (2) "God, in Christ, was reconciling the world," in which "in Christ" tells the means. The second is the likelier grammar, and the first is still true to other texts (Colossians 1:19; 2:9). The Plain keeps the familiar word order, "God was in Christ, reconciling," which can carry either reading. The "world" (kosmos) here is wider than the church. Whether this means all will be saved is argued, and the context speaks of the offer, "be reconciled" (5:20).

a: did not reckon their trespasses to them
t: Not reckoning sins: Psalm 32
p: Paul is using the language of Psalm 32, which he also quotes in Romans 4.
b: "Reckon" (logizomai) is a bookkeeping word, as in Romans 4, where Paul quotes Psalm 32: "Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never reckon" (Romans 4:8). Here God does not enter their trespasses into the ledger against them, because the account is settled in Christ. This language of not counting can also remind readers of the Day of Atonement, when the sins of the people were laid on the goat (Leviticus 16:21–22), which the next verse takes up (5:21).

t: Ambassadors: Rome's envoys
p: Paul uses a word for the emperor's envoys and for those who spoke for a king.
b: Presbeuo means to serve as an envoy (presbeutes), one who speaks for a ruler or a state. The emperor sent envoys to provinces and client kings, and cities sent them to Rome. An ambassador carried the authority of the one who sent him, and an insult to the envoy was an insult to the ruler. Paul uses the figure again in Ephesians 6:20 ("an ambassador in chains"). The ambassador's message here is not a threat but a plea: "be reconciled." Catholic tradition has found in the verse the basis for the priest's ministry (CCC 1442); Protestant tradition often applies it to every believer's witness.

t: "Made to be sin": how can that be?
p: Paul does not say Christ sinned. The phrase has been read as sin offering, as taking on our sin, or as taking on our place.
b: The words are among the shortest and hardest in the letter. Readings: (1) a sin offering, since the Greek Old Testament often says "sin" for the sin offering (hamartia for hatta't; Leviticus 4:3; Romans 8:3; Isaiah 53:10, "If his life is made a guilt offering"); (2) bearing the sin of others, like the goat that "will carry all their guilty deeds on itself to a land cut off" (Leviticus 16:22); (3) exchange: Christ takes our place, and we his (Hooker, Gorman); (4) Luther's strong form, "the greatest sinner," to say that Christ took all guilt on himself. All say "who did not know sin" means he was sinless. See the card.
r: Isaiah 53:4–6; Isaiah 53:10; Leviticus 16:21–22; Romans 8:3; Galatians 3:13; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22–24

t: "The righteousness of God" in him
p: Believers become "the righteousness of God." The phrase has been read as a gift, or as a task.
b: Romans uses the same phrase of God's own saving justice (Romans 1:17; 3:21–26). Here believers become it. Readings: (1) God's righteousness is counted or given to believers, whom God declares right (Reformed and Lutheran readings, drawing on Romans 4); (2) it is infused or worked in them, making them just (the Catholic reading, Trent session 6); (3) the apostles embody God's covenant faithfulness in their ministry of reconciliation, since "we" in 5:20–21 is the apostles (Wright, in an essay on this text); (4) a shared life in Christ (Orthodox participation, Gorman). The verse is the climax of 5:11–21.
